specStatements.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. The nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. This is a random process called radioactive decay.
Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decay s.
Activity is measured in becquerel (Bq)
Count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector (eg Geiger-Muller tube).
The nuclear radiation emitted may be:
• an alpha particle (α) – this consists of two neutrons and two protons, it is the same as a helium nucleus
• a beta particle (β) – a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton
• a gamma ray (γ) – electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus
• a neutron (n).
Required knowledge of the properties of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays is limited to their penetration through materials, their range in air and ionising power.
Students should be able to apply their knowledge to the uses of radiation and evaluate the best sources of radiation to use in a given situation.
Nuclear equations are used to represent radioactive decay.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol:
and a beta particle by the symbol:
The emission of the different types of nuclear radiation may cause a change in the mass and /or the charge of the nucleus. For example:
So alpha decay causes both the mass and charge of the nucleus to decrease.
So beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change but does cause the charge of the nucleus to increase.
Students are not required to recall these two examples.

Students should be able to use the names and symbols of common nuclei and particles to write balanced equations that show single alpha (α) and beta (β) decay. This is limited to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers. The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required.
The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
Radioactive decay is random.

The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample containing the isotope to fall to half its initial level.
Students should be able to explain the concept of half-life and how it is related to the random nature of radioactive decay.
Students should be able to determine the half-life of a radioactive isotope from given information.
(HT only) Students should be able to calculate the net decline, expressed as a ratio, in a radioactive emission after a given number of half-lives.

Radioactive contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms. The type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard.
Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.
Students should be able to compare the hazards associated with contamination and irradiation.
Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard that the radioactive source used in the process of irradiation may present.

Students should understand that it is important for the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans to be published and shared with other scientists so that the findings can be checked by peer review.

scopeNotes.statement: Required knowledge of the properties of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays is limited to their penetration through materials, their range in air and ionising power.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only those three properties are taught and tested: what each radiation is stopped by, how far it goes in air, and how strongly it ionises. Nothing here asks about deflection of the radiations in electric or magnetic fields, their charge-to-mass ratios, decay energies or energy spectra, half-value thickness, absorption coefficients, or the biological mechanism by which ionisation damages cells. Where a use of radiation is evaluated, the reasoning is built only from penetration, range in air and ionising power.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not required to recall these two examples.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The two worked decay examples printed in the specification are treated as illustrations of the general rules, not as facts to be memorised. No concept, misconception or question asks a student to state, reproduce or recognise those particular nuclides. The practice equations here deliberately use different nuclides so that success depends on balancing, not on recall of a specific example.

scopeNotes.statement: This is limited to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers. The identification of daughter elements from such decays is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every equation item asks only for the mass number and atomic number of the product nucleus, which is written as a general symbol X. No item requires a student to name the daughter element, to give its chemical symbol, or to consult a periodic table. Marks are therefore never dependent on element identification.

concepts.definition: Some atomic nuclei are unstable. Radioactive decay is the process in which such a nucleus gives out radiation as it changes to become more stable. It is a random process.
A nucleus that will not remain as it is. Because it is unstable it gives out radiation, and in doing so it changes to become more stable.

Radioactive decay is random: it is impossible to say which nucleus in a sample will decay next, or when any particular nucleus will decay. Only the behaviour of a large number of nuclei is predictable.
The rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays.
The unit in which activity is measured. An activity of 1 Bq is one decay per second, so a source of activity 300 Bq has 300 nuclei decaying each second.
The number of decays recorded each second by a detector. It is not the same as activity, because a detector only intercepts part of the radiation leaving the source.
The detector given by the specification as an example of an instrument that records decays. The number it records each second is the count-rate.

Nuclear radiation consisting of two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus. It has the shortest range in air and the greatest ionising power, and is stopped by a sheet of paper or by skin.
A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton. It has a range in air of about a metre and is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
Electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus. It has the greatest range in air and the lowest ionising power, and requires thick lead or concrete to reduce it substantially.
A neutron emitted from the nucleus. The specification lists a neutron alongside alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays as nuclear radiation that may be emitted.
How readily a radiation knocks electrons off the atoms it passes through. Alpha is the most ionising, beta less so, and gamma the least ionising.
How far a radiation gets into a material before it is absorbed. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, beta by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.
How far a radiation travels in air before it is absorbed. Alpha travels only a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma a very long distance.
An equation used to represent radioactive decay, showing the original nucleus on the left and the new nucleus together with the emitted particle on the right.
The upper number written before a nuclear symbol: the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus. The mass numbers must balance on the two sides of a nuclear equation.
The lower number written before a nuclear symbol: the number of protons in the nucleus, which sets its charge. The atomic numbers must balance on the two sides of a nuclear equation.
In a nuclear equation an alpha particle may be represented by the symbol ⁴₂He: mass number 4, atomic number 2.
In a nuclear equation a beta particle may be represented by the symbol ⁰₋₁e: mass number 0, and a lower number of −1 because the electron carries a charge of −1.
Emission of an alpha particle. The mass number of the nucleus falls by 4 and its atomic number falls by 2, so alpha decay causes both the mass and charge of the nucleus to decrease.
Emission of a beta particle. The mass number of the nucleus is unchanged and its atomic number rises by 1, so beta decay does not change the mass of the nucleus but does cause its charge to increase.
Emission of a gamma ray. It does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change, so the mass number and atomic number are both unaltered.
Checking that the mass numbers on the left add up to the mass numbers on the right, and that the atomic numbers do the same. For single alpha and beta decay this is all that is required.

The time it takes for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or the time it takes for the count rate (or activity) from a sample containing the isotope to fall to half its initial level.
After n half-lives the emission from a source has fallen to (1/2)ⁿ of its starting value, so the ratio of the final emission to the initial emission is 1 : 2ⁿ. After 3 half-lives this is 1 : 8.

The unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials. The hazard from contamination is due to the decay of the contaminating atoms, and the type of radiation emitted affects the level of hazard.
The process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation. The irradiated object does not become radioactive.

Suitable precautions must be taken to protect against any hazard that the radioactive source used in the process of irradiation may present, for example keeping the source in a lead-lined container, handling it with long tongs, standing well back and limiting the time of exposure.

The checking of published findings by other scientists. It is important for the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans to be published and shared so that they can be checked in this way.

concepts.term: Choosing a source for a use
concepts.definition: Selecting the radiation whose penetration, range in air and ionising power suit the job: alpha where the radiation must be absorbed almost at once, beta where it must pass through a thin layer, gamma where it must pass through a thick one.

misconceptions.question: Can you say when a particular unstable nucleus will decay?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radioactive decay is a random process, so it is impossible to predict which nucleus decays next or when a given nucleus will decay.
misconceptions.misconception: Each nucleus has a fixed lifetime, so if you knew enough about it you could work out the exact moment it will decay.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Half-life is quoted as a definite number, and decay curves are smooth, so decay looks like a clockwork process rather than a random one.
misconceptions.correction: The definite half-life is a statistical result from an enormous number of nuclei. For any single nucleus there is only a chance of decaying in the next second, never a scheduled time.

misconceptions.question: Is the count-rate from a detector the same as the activity of the source?
misconceptions.correct: No. Activity is the rate at which the source's unstable nuclei decay; count-rate is the number of decays recorded each second by a detector.
misconceptions.misconception: They are the same quantity with two different names, so the reading on the Geiger-Muller tube is the activity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are measured per second and both go down together, and school experiments treat count-rate as a stand-in for activity.
misconceptions.correction: A detector only occupies a small part of the space around the source, and some radiation is absorbed before it arrives, so the count-rate is normally well below the activity.

misconceptions.question: What does an activity of 500 Bq tell you?
misconceptions.correct: That 500 nuclei in the source decay each second. The becquerel measures the rate of decay.
misconceptions.misconception: It tells you how much energy the source gives out each second, or how much radioactive material it holds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet other 'per second' units such as the watt, and assume any radiation unit must be about energy or amount.
misconceptions.correction: Activity counts events, not energy or mass. Two sources can hold very different amounts of material and still both decay at 500 times per second.

misconceptions.question: What exactly is an alpha particle?
misconceptions.correct: Two neutrons and two protons; it is the same as a helium nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a helium atom, so it comes complete with two electrons around the outside.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'the same as helium' is remembered without the word nucleus, and helium is the familiar substance rather than the bare nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: Only the nucleus is emitted. The alpha particle has no electrons, which is why it carries a charge of +2 and is written ⁴₂He.

misconceptions.question: Where does a beta particle come from?
misconceptions.correct: It is a high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: It is one of the electrons orbiting the atom, which gets knocked out and flies off at speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know electrons live outside the nucleus, so an emitted electron seems bound to have come from there.
misconceptions.correction: The electron is created at the instant a neutron becomes a proton inside the nucleus. That is why the atomic number rises by 1, which could not happen if an orbiting electron simply left.

misconceptions.question: Does the nucleus contain a store of electrons ready to be emitted?
misconceptions.correct: No. The electron is produced at the moment a neutron in the nucleus turns into a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: The nucleus must keep some electrons inside it, otherwise there would be nothing there for it to emit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Emission is pictured as something coming out of a container, so students assume the object must have been inside beforehand.
misconceptions.correction: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons only. Beta emission is a change of one particle into another, not the release of something already stored.

misconceptions.question: Which part of the atom does nuclear radiation come from?
misconceptions.correct: The nucleus. Alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays and neutrons are all emitted from the nucleus.
misconceptions.misconception: Radiation is given off by the electrons when they drop down between energy levels, as it is for light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have met light being emitted by electrons changing levels, and transfer that picture to radioactivity.
misconceptions.correction: Radioactive decay is a change in the nucleus. Gamma radiation in particular is defined by the specification as electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus, not from the electrons.

misconceptions.question: Which radiation is the most ionising?
misconceptions.correct: Alpha is the most ionising, beta is less ionising, and gamma is the least ionising of the three.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma must be the most ionising, because it is the most penetrating and so the most dangerous one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Most penetrating' is heard as 'strongest', and 'strongest' is then assumed to mean worst in every respect.
misconceptions.correction: Gamma penetrates precisely because it interacts so little with the atoms it passes: weak interaction means low ionising power. Alpha is stopped quickly because it ionises so heavily on the way.

misconceptions.question: Is an alpha source harmless because paper stops it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alpha is easily blocked from outside the body, but it is the most hazardous if a source contaminates the inside of the body.
misconceptions.misconception: Alpha cannot even get through paper or skin, so an alpha source cannot really hurt anyone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The penetration facts are learned first and are usually demonstrated with the source outside the body, so the contamination case never gets considered.
misconceptions.correction: If alpha-emitting atoms are swallowed or breathed in there is no skin in the way. All the energy is deposited in a small volume of tissue, and its high ionising power makes it the most damaging radiation inside the body.

misconceptions.question: Does a more penetrating radiation ionise more strongly?
misconceptions.correct: No. The order of ionising power runs opposite to the order of penetration: alpha ionises most but penetrates least.
misconceptions.misconception: The more penetrating a radiation is, the more strongly it must ionise, since it goes through more material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both properties sound like measures of 'strength', so students expect them to increase together rather than trade off against each other.
misconceptions.correction: A radiation loses energy every time it ionises an atom. Heavy ionisation therefore uses up its energy quickly and stops it in a short distance, which is exactly why alpha does not penetrate.

misconceptions.question: Do alpha, beta and gamma travel similar distances in air?
misconceptions.correct: No. Alpha travels only a few centimetres, beta about a metre, and gamma travels a very long distance.
misconceptions.misconception: They all spread out through the room in much the same way, so the range in air is roughly the same for each.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In the laboratory all three set the counter clicking from the bench, so the differences in range are not obvious to a student watching.
misconceptions.correction: Move the detector back and the difference is stark: the alpha count falls away within a few centimetres, beta persists to about a metre, and gamma is still detectable far beyond that.

misconceptions.question: Can you slow a source's decay by cooling it or speed it up by heating it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Radioactive decay is a random nuclear process and is not affected by heating, cooling or chemical treatment.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating a source should make the nuclei more energetic, so it will decay faster; cooling it will slow the decay down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other rate students have met, from dissolving to reacting, depends on temperature, so decay is expected to behave the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Chemistry and temperature act on electrons, while decay happens in the nucleus. Nothing done in a school laboratory changes the chance that a given nucleus decays.

misconceptions.question: When you balance a nuclear equation, what has to match?
misconceptions.correct: Both the mass numbers and the atomic numbers must add up to the same total on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the top numbers have to add up; the bottom numbers can be left to look after themselves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass number is the number students check first and it is the one that most obviously has to be conserved, so the atomic number gets forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is conserved as well as mass. In beta decay the atomic numbers only balance because the beta particle counts as −1, which is the whole point of writing it as ⁰₋₁e.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the numbers when a nucleus emits an alpha particle?
misconceptions.correct: The mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number falls by 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass number falls by 2 and the atomic number falls by 4, because two protons and two neutrons leave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The figures 2 and 4 both appear in the description of an alpha particle, and students attach them to the wrong number of the pair.
misconceptions.correction: The alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so it removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number. Four nucleons leave in total, but only two of them are protons.

misconceptions.question: Does beta decay change the mass number of the nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. Beta decay does not cause the mass of the nucleus to change, but it does cause the charge to increase.
misconceptions.misconception: A new proton appears in the nucleus, so there is one more particle and the mass number goes up by 1.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track the proton being created and count it as an addition, forgetting that it was made out of a neutron that is no longer there.
misconceptions.correction: A neutron turns into a proton, so the total number of nucleons stays the same. The mass number is unchanged and only the atomic number rises by 1.

misconceptions.question: Does the atomic number go down in beta decay because a negative particle leaves?
misconceptions.correct: No. The atomic number increases by 1, because a neutron has turned into a proton.
misconceptions.misconception: Something negative has been emitted, so the nucleus must have lost charge and the atomic number must fall.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Losing an electron' is associated with the atom becoming positive, and the sign reasoning is applied to the wrong quantity.
misconceptions.correction: Atomic number counts protons, and the nucleus has gained one. Charge still balances because the emitted beta particle carries −1, which cancels the +1 gained by the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What does gamma emission do to the nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: Nothing to its mass or charge. The emission of a gamma ray does not cause the mass or the charge of the nucleus to change.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma emission must change the nucleus in some way, otherwise there would be no point in calling it decay.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alpha and beta are learned first and both change the numbers, so students generalise that every emission alters the nucleus.
misconceptions.correction: A gamma ray carries away energy only, and energy is not counted by the mass number or the atomic number. The nucleus becomes more stable while both numbers stay exactly the same.

misconceptions.question: What does half-life mean?
misconceptions.correct: The time for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve, or for the count rate or activity to fall to half its initial level.
misconceptions.misconception: It is half of the total time the source stays radioactive, so a half-life of 2 hours means the source is finished after 4 hours.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word is read as 'half of the life', and life is taken to mean the whole time the source lasts.
misconceptions.correction: Halving is repeated, not a one-off. After 2 hours half is left, after 4 hours a quarter, after 6 hours an eighth, and the sample never reaches exactly zero.

misconceptions.question: Is a sample completely decayed after two half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: No. After two half-lives a quarter of the original nuclei remain.
misconceptions.misconception: One half-life removes half and the second half-life removes the other half, so after two the sample has gone.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The halves are added rather than applied one after the other, which gives a total of one whole and an empty sample.
misconceptions.correction: The second half-life halves what is left, not what there was at the start. Half of a half is a quarter, and each further half-life halves the remainder again.

misconceptions.question: Does the half-life get shorter as the sample runs down?
misconceptions.correct: No. The half-life of a given isotope is constant, whatever the size or age of the sample.
misconceptions.misconception: As there are fewer nuclei left there is less to decay, so the halving must start taking longer or shorter as time goes on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect a fading process to change pace, and a decay curve does flatten, which looks like the process slowing down.
misconceptions.correction: The curve flattens because there are fewer nuclei, not because each one is less likely to decay. The time to lose half of what remains is the same at every point on the curve.

misconceptions.question: If decay is random, how can half-life have a definite value?
misconceptions.correct: Because a sample contains an enormous number of nuclei, so the average behaviour of the whole sample is highly predictable.
misconceptions.misconception: Randomness must make half-life a rough guess, so any half-life quoted is only an estimate of what might happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Random is taken to mean lawless, so students conclude nothing about a random process can be stated precisely.
misconceptions.correction: Randomness at the level of one nucleus produces reliable averages across many. It is like tossing a million coins: no single toss is predictable, yet close to half will come up heads every time.

misconceptions.question: A count-rate falls from 800 to 200 counts per second in 30 minutes. What is the half-life?
misconceptions.correct: 15 minutes. The count-rate has halved twice, from 800 to 400 and then from 400 to 200, so 30 minutes covers two half-lives.
misconceptions.misconception: The count-rate has dropped once, from 800 down to 200, so the half-life must be the whole 30 minutes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any single drop shown in the question is read as one halving, without checking how many times the number has actually been halved.
misconceptions.correction: Count the halvings, not the readings. 800 to 400 is one, 400 to 200 is two, so the 30 minutes must be divided by 2.

misconceptions.question: How do you get the half-life from the total time and the drop in count-rate?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the total time by the number of halvings, not by the factor the count-rate has fallen by.
misconceptions.misconception: The count-rate has fallen to a quarter over 30 minutes, so divide 30 by 4 to get the half-life.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The factor 4 is the most visible number in the problem, so it is used directly in the division instead of the count of halvings.
misconceptions.correction: A fall to a quarter is two halvings, so 30 minutes is divided by 2, giving 15 minutes. The factor and the number of half-lives are different things: a factor of 4 means 2 half-lives, a factor of 8 means 3.

misconceptions.question: Does an object that has been irradiated become radioactive?
misconceptions.correct: No. Irradiation is the process of exposing an object to nuclear radiation, and the irradiated object does not become radioactive.
misconceptions.misconception: Radiation must leave something behind in whatever it hits, so irradiated food or equipment must be radioactive afterwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Contamination and irradiation are lumped together, and radiation is imagined as a substance that sticks to whatever it touches.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation passing through an object transfers energy but leaves no radioactive atoms behind. Only contamination, which is unwanted radioactive material actually deposited on the object, makes it radioactive.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
misconceptions.correct: Contamination is the unwanted presence of materials containing radioactive atoms on other materials; irradiation is exposing an object to radiation from a source outside it.
misconceptions.misconception: They are two words for the same thing: any time radiation reaches you, you are both contaminated and irradiated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both terms appear together, both involve radiation and a person, and everyday speech uses 'contaminated' loosely for any exposure.
misconceptions.correction: The test is whether radioactive atoms are now on or in the object. Step away from a source and irradiation stops at once; contamination travels with you and keeps decaying.

misconceptions.question: What fraction of a sample remains after 4 half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: One sixteenth, because the amount is halved four times over: a half, a quarter, an eighth, a sixteenth.
misconceptions.misconception: Four half-lives means one quarter is left, since the fraction remaining is one over the number of half-lives.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number of half-lives is inserted straight into a fraction, because repeated halving is treated as division by the count.
misconceptions.correction: Each half-life multiplies what remains by a half, so the fractions multiply rather than the denominators counting up. After n half-lives the fraction left is (1/2) to the power n.

misconceptions.question: (HT) By what ratio has the emission declined after 4 half-lives?
misconceptions.correct: The emission has fallen to 1/16 of its original value, so the ratio of final to initial emission is 1 : 16.
misconceptions.misconception: Four half-lives means the emission is 8 times smaller, because you double the 4 to allow for the halving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is remembered as a piece of arithmetic involving 2 and the number of half-lives, and doubling feels more natural than raising 2 to a power.
misconceptions.correction: The factor is 2 raised to the number of half-lives, not 2 multiplied by it. Four half-lives gives 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 16, so the ratio is 1 : 16.

misconceptions.question: Why must studies of the effects of radiation on humans be published?
misconceptions.correct: So that other scientists can check the findings by peer review.
misconceptions.misconception: So that the public can read them and decide by consensus whether the results should be believed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Publication is associated with news coverage and public opinion rather than with scrutiny by specialists in the same field.
misconceptions.correction: Peer review means examination by other scientists working in the field, who can look for flaws in the method and try to repeat the work. Public opinion plays no part in checking whether a study is sound.

misconceptions.question: Does a Geiger-Muller tube record every decay that happens in a source?
misconceptions.correct: No. It records only the decays whose radiation happens to enter the tube, so the count-rate is lower than the activity.
misconceptions.misconception: The counter is designed to detect the source, so the number it shows each second is the number of decays each second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The count-rate is the only number a student can actually see in an experiment, so it is taken to be the full picture.
misconceptions.correction: Radiation leaves the source in all directions and the tube covers only a small part of them, so most decays are never recorded. Moving the tube changes the count-rate while the activity stays the same.

misconceptions.question: Is a neutron a type of nuclear radiation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The specification lists a neutron alongside alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays as radiation that may be emitted.
misconceptions.misconception: Only alpha, beta and gamma count as nuclear radiation; a neutron is just a particle that lives inside the nucleus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three Greek-letter radiations dominate lessons and revision, so the fourth item in the specification's list is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: The specification gives four types of nuclear radiation that may be emitted, and a neutron (n) is the fourth. A neutron can be emitted from a nucleus just as an alpha or beta particle can.

misconceptions.question: In the symbol ⁴₂He, what does the 4 count?
misconceptions.correct: The mass number: the total of 4 particles, made up of two protons and two neutrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The 4 counts the neutrons in the alpha particle, and the 2 counts the protons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The description 'two neutrons and two protons' contains two 2s, so the 4 has to be given a job, and neutrons are the nearest available.
misconceptions.correction: The upper figure is always the mass number, the total number of protons and neutrons. Here that total is 4, and the lower figure 2 gives the protons.

misconceptions.question: Would a lab coat and gloves protect you from a gamma source?
misconceptions.correct: No. Gamma is highly penetrating, so shielding needs thick lead or concrete, along with distance and short exposure times.
misconceptions.misconception: Protective clothing stops the radiation reaching you, so a lab coat and gloves are enough for any source.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Laboratory safety routines make clothing feel like the standard protection, and paper stopping alpha is generalised to every radiation.
misconceptions.correction: Cloth would stop alpha but is transparent to gamma. Suitable precautions for a gamma source are a lead-lined container, handling at a distance with tongs, and limiting the time of exposure.

misconceptions.question: Is a gamma ray a particle like alpha and beta?
misconceptions.correct: No. A gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus, so it has no mass number and no charge.
misconceptions.misconception: All three radiations come out of the nucleus, so gamma must be a small fast particle as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The three are always taught as a set and compared in the same table, which makes them look like three versions of one kind of thing.
misconceptions.correction: Alpha and beta are particles, but gamma is a wave in the electromagnetic spectrum. That is why gamma emission changes neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus.

misconceptions.question: Which source should be chosen for a job?
misconceptions.correct: The one whose penetration, range in air and ionising power match what the job needs.
misconceptions.misconception: The strongest source available, because more penetrating or more ionising radiation always does the job better.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Choosing 'the best' is read as choosing 'the most powerful', without asking what the radiation actually has to do.
misconceptions.correction: A thickness gauge needs radiation that partly gets through the material, so beta suits foil and gamma suits steel. A smoke alarm needs radiation absorbed within centimetres, so alpha is chosen precisely because it is weakly penetrating.

misconceptions.question: How do the alpha particle's numbers enter the balance?
misconceptions.correct: They are subtracted from the original nucleus: mass number falls by 4 and atomic number falls by 2.
misconceptions.misconception: The alpha particle's 4 and 2 are added to the numbers of the new nucleus so that everything adds up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is remembered as 'make both sides add up' without keeping track of which side the emitted particle now sits on.
misconceptions.correction: The alpha particle appears on the right of the equation, so its numbers come out of the parent's totals. Subtract to find the new nucleus, then check the two sides match.

misconceptions.question: Is a nuclear equation balanced in the same way as a chemical equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. A nuclear equation is balanced by making the mass numbers and the atomic numbers match on each side.
misconceptions.misconception: You balance it by making sure there are the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing equations is a skill first learned in chemistry, and the same procedure is applied without noticing that the element itself changes.
misconceptions.correction: In nuclear decay the element changes, so counting atoms of each element cannot work. Only the totals of mass number and atomic number are conserved.

misconceptions.question: Does each nucleus half-decay during a half-life?
misconceptions.correct: No. Half of the nuclei present decay completely; the rest are untouched.
misconceptions.misconception: Over one half-life every nucleus in the sample gets halfway through decaying.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word half is attached to the individual nucleus rather than to the population, and decay is imagined as gradual.
misconceptions.correction: A nucleus either decays or it does not; there is no partial decay. Half-life describes how many of them have decayed, not how far each one has got.

misconceptions.question: Why does a decay curve look so smooth if decay is random?
misconceptions.correct: Because so many nuclei are involved that the fluctuations are tiny compared with the total.
misconceptions.misconception: The nuclei must decay in some sort of order, taking turns, which is what makes the pattern regular.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A smooth graph suggests organisation, so students supply a mechanism that would produce it.
misconceptions.correction: There is no order and no queue. Each nucleus independently has the same chance of decaying, and averaging over billions of independent chances produces a smooth curve.

misconceptions.question: (HT) How should the net decline be written as a ratio?
misconceptions.correct: Final emission to initial emission, so a fall to one eighth is written 1 : 8.
misconceptions.misconception: The two numbers can be written either way round, so 8 : 1 means the same as 1 : 8.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ratios are treated as a pair of numbers rather than as an ordered comparison, so the order is thought not to matter.
misconceptions.correction: Order carries the meaning. 1 : 8 says the emission is now one eighth of what it was; 8 : 1 would say it is eight times greater. State clearly which quantity comes first.

misconceptions.question: Does publication mean the findings are correct?
misconceptions.correct: No. Publication allows other scientists to check the findings by peer review.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a study on radiation has been published it has been proved right, so the conclusion is settled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Print carries authority, and students take publication as the end of the process rather than the start of the checking.
misconceptions.correction: Publishing exposes the work to scrutiny. Other scientists can examine the method and try to repeat it, and findings can be revised or rejected as a result.

mcqs.stem: A sample of rock contains unstable nuclei. Which statement best describes radioactive decay?

options.text: Each nucleus gives out radiation at a set time that can be predicted.
options.rationale: Half-lives are quoted as exact figures, so decay is pictured as scheduled rather than random.

options.text: The nucleus gives out radiation only when the sample is heated strongly.
options.rationale: Every other rate a student has met depends on temperature, so decay is assumed to as well.

options.text: Radiation comes from the electrons as they move closer to the nucleus.
options.rationale: Light emission by electrons changing energy level is transferred to radioactivity.

options.text: A nucleus gives out radiation at random as it becomes more stable.
options.rationale: Matches the specification: unstable nuclei give out radiation as they change to become more stable, and the process is random.

mcqs.stem: What does the activity of a radioactive source measure, and in what unit?

options.text: The energy given out by the source each second, in becquerel.
options.rationale: Other 'per second' quantities are about energy, so the becquerel is assumed to be as well.

options.text: The rate at which unstable nuclei decay, measured in becquerel.
options.rationale: Activity is the rate at which a source of unstable nuclei decays, and it is measured in becquerel (Bq).

options.text: The number of decays a detector records each second, in becquerel.
options.rationale: This defines count-rate, which students routinely treat as the same thing as activity.

options.text: The number of unstable nuclei left in the source, in becquerel.
options.rationale: Activity is confused with the quantity of radioactive material rather than the rate of decay.

mcqs.stem: A Geiger-Muller tube is set up near a radioactive source. What does its reading give?

options.text: The activity: every decay happening in the source each second.
options.rationale: Activity and count-rate are treated as interchangeable because both are quoted per second.

options.text: The energy carried by each decay, added up over one second.
options.rationale: The detector is imagined as an energy meter rather than an event counter.

options.text: The total number of decays since the source was first made.
options.rationale: A running total is confused with a rate; the reading is per second, not cumulative.

options.text: The count-rate: the number of decays recorded each second.
options.rationale: Count-rate is defined by the specification as the number of decays recorded each second by a detector.

mcqs.stem: What is an alpha particle?

options.text: A helium atom, complete with its two orbiting electrons.
options.rationale: 'The same as helium' is remembered without the crucial word nucleus.

options.text: Four neutrons bound together, which is why its mass is 4.
options.rationale: The 4 in the symbol is taken to be a count of neutrons rather than the mass number.

options.text: Two neutrons and two protons, the same as a helium nucleus.
options.rationale: This is exactly how the specification defines an alpha particle.

options.text: Two protons and two electrons bound inside the nucleus.
options.rationale: The nucleus is imagined as containing electrons available for emission.

mcqs.stem: What is a beta particle and where does it come from?

options.text: A high speed electron ejected from the nucleus as a neutron turns into a proton.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition, and it explains why the atomic number rises by 1.

options.text: An electron from the outer shells of the atom that escapes at high speed.
options.rationale: Electrons are known to live outside the nucleus, so that is where the beta particle is assumed to start.

options.text: An electron that had been stored inside the nucleus and is simply released.
options.rationale: Emission is pictured as release from a store rather than as one particle changing into another.

options.text: A high speed proton ejected from the nucleus as it becomes more stable.
options.rationale: The proton is the particle created in beta decay, so it is mistaken for the particle emitted.

mcqs.stem: What is a gamma ray?

options.text: Electromagnetic radiation emitted by orbiting electrons.
options.rationale: Emission of light by electrons changing level is transferred to nuclear radiation.

options.text: A heavy, fast-moving particle emitted by the nucleus.
options.rationale: Gamma is grouped with alpha and beta and so assumed to be a particle too.

options.text: A stream of high speed neutrons released by a nucleus.
options.rationale: Two different entries in the specification's list of radiations are merged.

options.text: Electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus.
options.rationale: The specification defines a gamma ray as electromagnetic radiation from the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: Besides alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays, which of these does the specification list as nuclear radiation that may be emitted?

options.text: A neutron from the nucleus
options.rationale: The specification's list of nuclear radiation is alpha particle, beta particle, gamma ray and neutron.

options.text: A proton from the nucleus
options.rationale: The fourth item is remembered as some nuclear particle, and proton is chosen instead of neutron.

options.text: An electron from a shell
options.rationale: An emitted electron is assumed to come from outside the nucleus.

options.text: An X-ray from the nucleus
options.rationale: X-rays are known as ionising radiation, so they are assumed to be on the nuclear list.

mcqs.stem: Which list puts the three radiations in order of ionising power, most ionising first?

options.text: gamma, then beta, then alpha
options.rationale: Gamma is thought to be the most dangerous and therefore the most ionising.

options.text: gamma, then alpha, then beta
options.rationale: Penetration and ionising power are assumed to run in the same direction.

options.text: beta, then alpha, then gamma
options.rationale: Beta is placed in the middle of the penetration order and then assumed to lead here.

options.text: alpha, then beta, then gamma
options.rationale: Alpha is the most ionising, beta intermediate, gamma the least.

mcqs.stem: A radiation from a source is completely stopped by a sheet of paper. Which radiation is it, and what is its range in air?

options.text: Beta, and it travels roughly one metre through the air.
options.rationale: The stopping material is misremembered; beta needs a few millimetres of aluminium.

options.text: Gamma, and paper absorbs it so its range is short.
options.rationale: Gamma is treated as the radiation that everything blocks or nothing blocks, inconsistently.

options.text: Alpha, but it still travels many metres through air.
options.rationale: The penetration fact is known but the range in air is assumed to be similar for all.

options.text: Alpha, and it travels only a few centimetres in air.
options.rationale: Alpha is stopped by paper and has a range in air of only a few centimetres.

mcqs.stem: A gauge controls the thickness of aluminium foil by detecting radiation that has passed through it. Which source is the best choice?

options.text: A gamma source, because gamma is the most penetrating and gives the strongest signal.
options.rationale: The most penetrating source is assumed to be the best for every job.

options.text: An alpha source, because alpha is the most ionising and is detected most easily.
options.rationale: Ionising power is treated as a measure of usefulness regardless of the task.

options.text: A beta source, because beta is completely stopped by even the thinnest foil.
options.rationale: The right source is chosen for the wrong reason: total absorption would give no signal.

options.text: A beta source, because some beta gets through and the amount varies with thickness.
options.rationale: Beta is partly absorbed by thin foil, so the count-rate responds to changes in thickness.

mcqs.stem: A smoke alarm contains a source that ionises the air in a small gap inside it. Which source is suitable and why?

options.text: Alpha, because it ionises strongly and cannot travel far from the alarm.
options.rationale: Alpha ionises the air strongly and its few-centimetre range keeps it inside the alarm.

options.text: Gamma, because it is the most penetrating so it fills the whole room.
options.rationale: The strongest and most penetrating source is assumed to be the best choice.

options.text: Beta, because it ionises the air well and has a range of about a metre.
options.rationale: Beta's ionising power is overstated and its escape from the alarm is ignored.

options.text: Gamma, because it is the least ionising and so is the safest at home.
options.rationale: Safety is judged on one property alone, ignoring gamma's penetration.

mcqs.stem: In a nuclear equation an alpha particle is written ⁴₂He. What do the 4 and the 2 represent?

options.text: 4 is the number of neutrons and 2 is the number of protons.
options.rationale: The description 'two neutrons and two protons' is mapped onto the wrong figures.

options.text: 4 is the mass number and 2 is the atomic number of the particle.
options.rationale: The upper figure is always the mass number and the lower figure the atomic number.

options.text: 4 is the atomic number and 2 is the mass number of the particle.
options.rationale: The positions of mass number and atomic number are reversed.

options.text: 4 is the charge on the particle and 2 is the number of nucleons.
options.rationale: Both figures are assigned to the wrong quantities, with charge read from the top.

mcqs.stem: A beta particle is written ⁰₋₁e in a nuclear equation. Why is the lower figure −1?

options.text: Because the nucleus loses one nucleon each time a beta particle leaves.
options.rationale: Nucleon counting is applied to the lower figure, which records charge not mass.

options.text: Because the beta particle carries a charge of −1, so the charges balance.
options.rationale: The lower figure is the charge, and −1 is what makes the atomic numbers balance.

options.text: Because the atomic number of the decaying nucleus falls by one here.
options.rationale: Beta decay is assumed to reduce the atomic number because a negative leaves.

options.text: Because the mass number of a beta particle is one less than zero.
options.rationale: The two figures in the symbol are confused with one another.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits an alpha particle. What happens to its mass number and atomic number?

options.text: Mass number falls by 2 and the atomic number falls by 4.
options.rationale: The 2 and the 4 in the description of an alpha particle are attached the wrong way round.

options.text: Mass number falls by 4 and atomic number falls by 2.
options.rationale: The alpha particle is ⁴₂He, so 4 is removed from the mass number and 2 from the atomic number.

options.text: Mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number rises by 2.
options.rationale: The alpha particle's figures are added to the daughter instead of subtracted.

options.text: Mass number stays the same and atomic number falls by 2.
options.rationale: Only the loss of the two protons is counted; the two neutrons are forgotten.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits a beta particle. What happens to its mass number and atomic number?

options.text: Mass number stays the same and atomic number decreases by 1.
options.rationale: A negative particle leaving is assumed to lower the nucleus's charge.

options.text: Mass number increases by 1 and atomic number increases by 1.
options.rationale: The new proton is counted as an extra particle rather than a converted neutron.

options.text: Mass number is unchanged and atomic number increases by 1.
options.rationale: A neutron becomes a proton, so the nucleon total holds and the proton count rises.

options.text: Mass number decreases by 1 and atomic number stays the same.
options.rationale: The emitted particle is treated as though it removed a nucleon from the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to the mass and the charge of the nucleus?

options.text: The mass stays the same but the charge decreases by 1.
options.rationale: Gamma is assumed to alter the nucleus because alpha and beta both do.

options.text: The mass decreases by 4 and the charge decreases by 2.
options.rationale: Gamma is treated as a particle that carries mass and charge away.

options.text: Neither the mass nor the charge of the nucleus changes.
options.rationale: The specification states that gamma emission does not change the mass or charge.

options.text: The mass stays the same but the charge increases by 1.
options.rationale: The change caused by beta decay is applied to gamma emission.

mcqs.stem: ²²⁶₈₈Ra decays by emitting an alpha particle. Which nuclear equation is balanced?

options.text: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²⁴₈₄X + ⁴₂He
options.rationale: The 4 and the 2 have been subtracted from the wrong figures.

options.text: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₉₀X + ⁴₂He
options.rationale: The alpha particle's atomic number has been added rather than subtracted.

options.text: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆X + ⁴₂He
options.rationale: 226 = 222 + 4 and 88 = 86 + 2, so both mass numbers and atomic numbers balance.

options.text: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²⁶₈₆X + ⁴₂He
options.rationale: Only the atomic numbers have been balanced; the mass numbers have been left alone.

mcqs.stem: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr decays by emitting a beta particle. Which nuclear equation is balanced?

options.text: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₇X + ⁰₋₁e
options.rationale: The atomic number has been reduced because a negative particle was emitted.

options.text: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹⁰₃₉X + ⁰₋₁e
options.rationale: 90 = 90 + 0 and 38 = 39 + (−1), so both totals balance.

options.text: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁹¹₃₉X + ⁰₋₁e
options.rationale: The new proton has been counted as an extra nucleon, raising the mass number.

options.text: ⁹⁰₃₈Sr → ⁸⁹₃₈X + ⁰₋₁e
options.rationale: The emitted particle is treated as taking a nucleon away from the nucleus.

mcqs.stem: When writing a balanced nuclear equation for a single alpha or beta decay, what must balance?

options.text: The mass numbers only, since the atomic numbers are free to change.
options.rationale: Mass number is checked first and the atomic number is then forgotten.

options.text: The number of atoms of each element, as in a chemical equation.
options.rationale: The chemistry procedure for balancing is carried across unchanged.

options.text: The mass numbers and the atomic numbers on each side of the equation.
options.rationale: The specification limits this skill to balancing the atomic numbers and mass numbers.

options.text: The total energy released and the mass numbers on both sides.
options.rationale: Energy conservation is introduced into a balance that only counts nucleons and charge.

mcqs.stem: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?

options.text: The time for the whole sample of the isotope to finish decaying away.
options.rationale: 'Half-life' is read as the lifetime of the source rather than a halving time.

options.text: The time for the count rate from the sample to fall to zero counts.
options.rationale: Decay is imagined as running to completion in a fixed time.

options.text: The time for the number of nuclei of the isotope in a sample to halve.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition, which can equally be given in terms of count rate or activity.

options.text: The time for half of each individual nucleus in the sample to decay.
options.rationale: The word half is attached to each nucleus instead of to the population.

mcqs.stem: Radioactive decay is random, yet a half-life has a definite value. Why?

options.text: A sample holds a vast number of nuclei, so the average behaviour is predictable.
options.rationale: Randomness for individual nuclei produces a reliable average across very large numbers.

options.text: Randomness only applies to single nuclei, so any half-life quoted is a rough guess.
options.rationale: Random is taken to mean that nothing precise can be stated at all.

options.text: The nuclei decay one after another in turn, which is what makes it regular.
options.rationale: A smooth decay curve is explained by supposing the nuclei are organised.

options.text: The detector averages its readings, and that removes the randomness entirely.
options.rationale: The regularity is attributed to the instrument rather than to large numbers.

mcqs.stem: The count-rate from a source is 800 counts per second. Thirty minutes later it is 200 counts per second. What is the half-life?

options.text: 30 minutes
options.rationale: The single drop from 800 to 200 is counted as one halving.

options.text: 7.5 minutes
options.rationale: The 30 minutes is divided by the factor of 4 instead of by the two halvings.

options.text: 15 minutes
options.rationale: 800 to 400 to 200 is two halvings in 30 minutes, so one half-life is 15 minutes.

options.text: 10 minutes
options.rationale: The 30 minutes is divided by three, as though three halvings had occurred.

mcqs.stem: The activity of a sample falls to 25% of its starting value in 12 hours. What is the half-life?

options.text: 12 hours
options.rationale: The whole fall is treated as a single halving.

options.text: 3 hours
options.rationale: 25% is read as four half-lives, so 12 is divided by 4.

options.text: 4 hours
options.rationale: The 12 hours is divided by the factor of 4 rather than by the number of halvings.

options.text: 6 hours
options.rationale: A fall to 25% is two halvings, so each half-life takes 12 divided by 2 = 6 hours.

mcqs.stem: A sample has a half-life of 5 days. What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 20 days?

options.rationale: The number of half-lives is placed straight into the fraction.
20 days is four half-lives, and halving four times leaves one sixteenth.
The number of days is used in the fraction instead of the number of half-lives.
Only three halvings are counted instead of four.

mcqs.stem: (HT) After 4 half-lives, what is the ratio of the emission from a source to its original emission?

options.rationale: Four halvings give a factor of 2 to the power 4, which is 16.
The factor is taken as 2 multiplied by 4 rather than 2 raised to the power 4.
The correct factor is found but the ratio is written the wrong way round.
The number of half-lives is used directly as the factor.

mcqs.stem: (HT) A count-rate falls from 6400 to 200 counts per second. What is the ratio of the final count-rate to the initial one, and how many half-lives have passed?

options.text: 1 : 10, after 5 half-lives
options.rationale: The number of half-lives is correct but the factor is taken as 2 multiplied by 5.

options.text: 32 : 1, after 5 half-lives
options.rationale: The arithmetic is right but the ratio is stated the wrong way round.

options.text: 1 : 32, after 6 half-lives
options.rationale: The halvings are miscounted by one when working down from 6400.

options.text: 1 : 32, after 5 half-lives
options.rationale: 6400 divided by 200 is 32, and 32 is 2 to the power 5, so five half-lives have passed.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes contamination from irradiation?

options.text: Irradiation leaves an object radioactive, while contamination does not do so.
options.rationale: Radiation is imagined as a substance that is left behind in whatever it strikes.

options.text: Contamination puts radioactive atoms onto an object; irradiation only exposes it.
options.rationale: Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive materials; irradiation is exposure to radiation.

options.text: Contamination is exposure to radiation; irradiation means swallowing a source.
options.rationale: The two terms are known but their meanings have been swapped over.

options.text: Contamination happens outdoors, while irradiation happens in a laboratory.
options.rationale: The distinction is made by setting rather than by what has happened to the object.

mcqs.stem: Strawberries are irradiated with gamma rays to kill bacteria. Are the strawberries now radioactive?

options.text: Yes, the gamma rays leave radioactive atoms in the fruit.
options.rationale: Radiation is thought to deposit radioactive material wherever it goes.

options.text: No, an irradiated object does not become radioactive.
options.rationale: The specification states plainly that the irradiated object does not become radioactive.

options.text: Yes, but only while the gamma source is still switched on.
options.rationale: Radioactivity is imagined as a temporary state induced by exposure.

options.text: No, because this counts as contamination, not irradiation.
options.rationale: The two terms are swapped, so the right answer is reached by wrong reasoning.

mcqs.stem: A source is accidentally swallowed, contaminating the body. Which emitter is now the most hazardous, and why?

options.text: An alpha emitter, because it ionises strongly and is all absorbed inside.
options.rationale: Inside the body there is no skin in the way, and alpha's high ionising power damages a small volume heavily.

options.text: An alpha emitter, because it is harmless outside but penetrates well inside.
options.rationale: The right emitter is chosen but alpha's penetration is misunderstood.

options.text: A gamma emitter, because gamma is the most penetrating of the radiations.
options.rationale: Penetration is treated as the only measure of hazard, inside or outside.

options.text: A beta emitter, because beta passes through tissue and out of the body.
options.rationale: Radiation leaving the body is taken as evidence of greater harm, not less.

mcqs.stem: A technician uses a gamma source to irradiate equipment. Which precaution is most suitable?

options.text: Store the source in a lead-lined container and handle it with long tongs.
options.rationale: Thick lead shielding plus distance are suitable precautions against a penetrating gamma source.

options.text: Wear a cotton laboratory coat, which will absorb the gamma radiation.
options.rationale: Protective clothing is assumed to stop radiation of any type.

options.text: Hold the source in a gloved hand so that the exposure time stays short.
options.rationale: Gloves are treated as shielding and a short time as sufficient protection.

options.text: Keep the source in a sealed paper envelope whenever it is not in use.
options.rationale: The fact that paper stops alpha is generalised to gamma as well.

mcqs.stem: Why should the findings of studies into the effects of radiation on humans be published and shared?

options.text: So that the public can vote on whether the findings should stand.
options.rationale: Publication is associated with public opinion rather than expert scrutiny.

options.text: Because publication proves that the findings are true and final.
options.rationale: Print is taken as an authority, so publication is read as the end of checking.

options.text: So that other scientists can check the findings by peer review.
options.rationale: The specification requires students to understand that publication allows checking by peer review.

options.text: So that the scientists involved are paid properly for their work.
options.rationale: Publication is confused with the funding and reward side of research.

mcqs.stem: Why is the count-rate measured near a source usually much lower than the source's activity?

options.text: The detector only catches part of the radiation leaving the source.
options.rationale: Radiation goes in all directions and the tube covers only a small fraction of them.

options.text: The count-rate equals the activity, so this situation can never arise.
options.rationale: Count-rate and activity are treated as the same quantity under two names.

options.text: Some nuclei decay without giving out anything a detector could catch.
options.rationale: An extra decay mode is invented to explain the difference in the figures.

options.text: Activity is measured in becquerel but count-rate is measured in joules.
options.rationale: The becquerel is thought to be an energy unit, so the two are on different scales.
